problem: On ALFRED, end-to-end models that map instructions and pixels directly to primitive actions (Seq2Seq, HAM, MOCA) generalize poorly: the previous best reaches below 10% success in unseen scenes, against over 90% for humans. These models are also opaque, so it is hard to tell which part of the task fails.
motivation: Household tasks are naturally hierarchical: a goal breaks into sub-goals such as Goto, Pickup and Clean, and each sub-goal breaks into navigation or manipulation primitives, much like an HTN plan. Making this structure explicit should let the agent check whether a sub-goal succeeded and re-plan when it did not. It also turns the benchmark into separable sub-problems that can be diagnosed one at a time. The three sub-problems share the same kinds of input (vision, language, symbolic predicates), which suggests one multi-task model can handle all of them.
key_idea: Split ALFRED into sub-goal planning, navigation and manipulation, and solve all three with one RoBERTa-initialized multi-task transformer. Its inputs are detected objects, instructions and predicate-history tokens. When a manipulation sub-goal fails, the explicit sub-goals let the agent backtrack to the preceding Goto sub-goal and try a different path.
insight:
Most of the gain comes from self-monitoring and backtracking, not from better single-shot prediction.
- Without backtracking, val-unseen SR is 5.2. It rises monotonically to 16.2 with 8 allowed backtracks (Table 4).
- Goto sub-goal success in unseen scenes rises from 31 to 65 (Table 5).
- Backtracking widens the gap between plain and path-length-weighted scores, because it turns instruction following into goal-oriented exploration.

The oracle study (Table 6) shows navigation is the bottleneck:
- Oracle sub-goals add only about 2–6 points of SR.
- Oracle navigation adds about 50 (seen) and 46 (unseen) absolute points.
- With oracle sub-goals, navigation and grounding (SG+N+GR), SR is about 99%. So predicting manipulation type and argument is trivial; visual grounding and navigation are the hard parts.

Learning-curve analyses (figure only) show two things:
- Removing vision does not hurt sub-goal or manipulation prediction.
- Removing language costs only 1–2% on action prediction.
This suggests heavy dataset bias and questions how much ALFRED's step instructions matter.
method: Hierarchical decomposition: the sub-goal planner M_sg(v_t, G, sg_<i) predicts sub-goal type and argument separately, online after each sub-goal is executed. The navigation model M_n(v_t, I_i, sg_i, a^n_<j) predicts one of RotateLeft/RotateRight/MoveAhead/LookUp/LookDown. The manipulation model M_m(v_t, I_i, sg_i, a^m_<j) predicts action type, action argument and an object mask.

Unified multi-task transformer: a single RoBERTa-initialized encoder has multiple heads (sub-goal type and argument, action type and argument, mask selection). It is trained MT-DNN style, sampling a batch from a random sub-problem at each iteration. Prediction history is fed as input tokens instead of a recurrent state. Training uses cross-entropy imitation learning on expert demos (10 epochs, Adam, peak lr 1e-5).

Predicate embedding: each symbol (e.g. AppleSliced) is mapped to a natural-language phrase ('a sliced apple'), and the word embeddings of its tokens are summed. This shares linguistic knowledge between symbols and words.

Detection-based vision encoding: two Mask R-CNNs, COCO-pretrained and fine-tuned on 50K ALFRED replay images, detect movable objects and receptacles separately. The top-K detections with score above 0.4 are kept. Each is encoded as its class word embedding plus a linear projection of a 7-d vector (box coordinates, width, height, confidence).

Object grounding by selection: the model picks one of the K detected objects and uses that detector's mask. The training label is the proposal with the highest IoU above 0.5 with the ground truth, or 0 if none qualifies. The fixed detector therefore upper-bounds grounding.
Posture feature: the agent's relative rotation (N/S/E/W) and horizon angle (15° bins) are embedded and summed. It is tracked relative to the start pose, with no extra sensors.

Self-monitoring and backtracking: a manipulation sub-goal is judged failed if any action fails to execute, or if no mask is selected, or if the predicted argument disagrees with the detector's class for the chosen object. On failure the agent backtracks to the preceding Goto sub-goal and tries a different primitive sequence, up to 8 backtracks. It also uses MOCA's obstruction-detection trick.

setting.backbone: RoBERTa transformer encoder (fine-tuned, multi-task) + two Mask R-CNN detectors (COCO-pretrained, fine-tuned on ALFRED)
setting.training_data: ALFRED train split expert demonstrations (6,574 demos / 21,023 annotations; 162k sub-goal, 983k navigation and 209k manipulation step instances). Mask R-CNN fine-tuned on 50K images collected by replaying ALFRED train expert trajectories. RoBERTa and COCO pretraining.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (processed into Mask R-CNN detections), goal directive + step-by-step instructions, relative agent posture (rotation, horizon angle)
setting.action_space: hierarchical: symbolic sub-goals → low-level discrete navigation (RotateLeft, RotateRight, MoveAhead, LookUp, LookDown) and manipulation actions (type + argument + selected object mask)
setting.privileged: none (training labels come from simulator metadata; test uses RGB only)

numbers_note: Table 4 (backtracking sweep) and the appendix pretraining table remove the 10-failed-interaction limit. As a result, #BT=8 there gives SR 27.2 (seen) / 16.2 (unseen), slightly above the Table 2 main results. Other results not listed: manipulation sub-goal success (Table 3: avg 88 seen / 81 unseen), Goto sub-goal success vs #backtracks (Table 5), oracle-replacement analysis (Table 6), and per-task-type success (appendix). Step-level prediction accuracy vs training-data fraction is shown only in a figure; the text gives only >90% / >98% accuracy with 5% of the data for sub-goal / manipulation, and 82% for navigation with all data.
results: On ALFRED test-unseen, HiTUT reaches SR 13.87 / GC 20.31, vs MOCA's 5.30 / 14.28, a gain of over 160% in unseen success rate. On test-seen it is comparable to MOCA (21.27 vs 22.05 SR), and on val-unseen it gets 12.44 SR vs MOCA's 3.78. Using only the goal directive (G only), it still gets 11.12 SR on test-unseen. Backtracking roughly triples val-unseen SR (5.2 → 16.2 with 8 backtracks), but path-length-weighted scores stay low (PLWSR 5.86 on test-unseen).
limitations: Grounding is bounded by a fixed pre-trained Mask R-CNN: the model can only choose among detected masks, and the detector is not improved during training.

Navigation remains the bottleneck (82% step accuracy; oracle navigation adds about 46–50 SR points). Backtracking compensates through extra exploration, which inflates path length and lowers path-length-weighted scores.

Navigation success cannot be verified directly; it is inferred only from whether the next manipulation succeeds. The findings on dataset bias (vision and language barely matter for planning) suggest the gains may partly reflect ALFRED-specific regularities.
